en: Preface to the *Jingang jing huijie liaoyi* (An Exegesis on the Diamond Sutra Clarifying the Definitive Meaning):
In the year Wuchen, while serving as a Vice Commissioner at the imperial residence in Yanjing, I began reciting the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. Thirty-five years have passed since then;

though my lips have recited it, my mind has remained without understanding. Desiring to resolve this lack of understanding through understanding, I realized from the outset that it could not be resolved by such means.
That cannot be understood; yet it is not that there is something that can be understood. There is that which is unresolvable, and I privately marvel at its profound flavor:
how can it be so deep and abstruse? It is ultimately without shallowness—how then can there be depth? It is without manifestation—how then can there be profundity?

On a grand scale, this is the world; on a minute scale, this is a mote of dust. It is clearly manifest enough to be pointed out, yet clearly manifest enough that nothing can be pointed out. How manifold!
Thus they arise in this manner. Briefly summarized, these are the four marks: truly there is attachment, yet truly there is nothing to which one is attached;
phenomena can be described, yet fundamentally phenomena have no existence; even when described together, there is no description.

Objects can be measured, yet objects have no substantiality; even when measured together, it is not measurement. Above, regarding the bestowal of prophecy, there is no prophecy; below, regarding the upholding [of the Dharma], there is no...
Uphold it. To expound even a four-line verse from within [this teaching] is to expound from no source;
all marks are not established, returning to non-self. Where conditioned activity does not arise, it is extinguished in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

In sum, there is no dharma upon which to dwell, and thus no mind that can dwell. This mind that dwells yet is without dwelling is precisely the dharma of "conquering without conquering. Therefore, protect it.
My remonstrances were not lacking in earnestness, yet in coming and going, sitting and reclining, there was previously no fixed standard.
My instructions were not lacking in urgency, yet among dreams, illusions, bubbles, and shadows, who is truly real? I have searched through all existing commentaries;

they do nothing more than harmonize the phrasing and extract the meaning, merely picking out chapters and lines. Within them, I have eliminated what is cumbersome, corrected what is erroneous, and clarified what is obscure.
That which is inverted is set right; that which calls and responds before and after has its words clarified; that which transforms between the void and the real has its meaning made accessible.
This means to directly trace back to the assembly on Vulture Peak, where [the truth] was revealed face-to-face and received face-to-face: the World-Honored One’s "not speaking is speaking."
Subhūti heard what cannot be heard. Ānanda compiled [the teachings] while the assembly was still solemnly gathered;
he captured the atmosphere of that very day. As for me, how would I dare? If one were to use the diamond as a metaphor for firmness and sharpness, I would say:
nothing is firmer than this mind, and nothing is sharper than this mind of faith in the Dharma. The light of the mind is itself the light of the Buddha; it belongs to every person.
There is the realization of *prajñā* (wisdom) that is manifest; it is realized through the mind rather than through the Buddha. Everywhere there are swift sūtras of the six *pāramitās*.
As for that which is nameless yet named—the true ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) where description is difficult—it is as they say:
"The sun rises in the west and sets in the east at night; the peach blossoms are white and the plum blossoms are red. How could this alone not be so?
Written by Xu Changzhi at Daye Hall during the final month of spring in the Xinchou year of the Shunzhi era,
as a preface to the *Jingang jing huijie liao yi* (An Exegesis on the Diamond Sutra Clarifying its Definitive Meaning).
Originally translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva;
revised by his elder brother Xu Congzhì (shoulder and neck), father Xu Guāngzhì (Mǎng and Xūn), and jointly edited by the Wayman Xu Chāngzhì (Jìn and Zhōu). Compiled.
Men: Xu Shengzhen, Xu Qianzhen, Xu Gongshu; Sons:
Xu Yizhen, Xu Chuyuan; Jointly proofread the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
The two characters "Vajra" (金剛) reveal the Buddha’s singular Vajra-mind, which is capable of severing doubt.
Because people of the world cannot understand the Buddha, nor his daily activities and conduct—each of which differs from those of ordinary men—they inevitably perceive him with suspicion.
Even among his own disciples, there were those who doubted the Dharma he taught, finding it difficult to believe and difficult to comprehend. Now...

"O Śāriputra, you were fortunate to catch even a glimpse of the World-Honored One; thus, you spontaneously gave rise to praise. Therefore, the World-Honored One, by means of your doubt, shattered it for you.
He then revealed a fragment of his own adamantine mind, causing all who heard it to have their manifold doubts suddenly severed.
Furthermore, this was able to sever the afflictions of sentient beings; thus, Maitreya’s twenty-seven doubts were severed, and he gave rise to the Unsurpassed [Enlightenment]."
Regarding the remaining meaning:
The Buddha preached the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* in six hundred fascicles across sixteen assemblies. This is the five hundred and seventy-seventh fascicle of that sūtra.
At the Jeta Grove, during the ninth assembly, the Vajra was held by the powerful Mārṣa Dharmapāla.

This is like a precious jade scepter, extremely hard and extremely sharp, such that there is nothing it cannot break. Hardness is used as a metaphor for the essence of *prajñā*, and sharpness as a metaphor for its function.
*Prajñā* is called "wisdom" (*hui*); it is the light of immovable gnosis, a luminous and divine illumination that is shared by every person.
The true nature of original enlightenment (*prakṛti-pratibhāsa*).
Regarding *pāramitā*: it means "reaching the other shore. Seeing one's nature and attaining liberation is itself the other shore; those who have not yet attained liberation [have not yet reached it].
This is precisely this shore. In reality, the other shore is one’s own inherent ground; it is the ultimate limit of this very mind.
The karmic consciousness of sentient beings drifts through a vast and boundless sea of suffering. Yet, a sea must necessarily flow from its shore; likewise, afflictions originally [arise] from...
Wisdom arises. By transforming boundless afflictions into boundless wisdom, one finally reaches the other shore.

This reaching is fundamentally no reaching; it is only that the deluded do not awaken to it themselves. (The *Prajñāpāramitā* says that wisdom destroys ignorance. Since both wisdom and ignorance lack a fixed essence, if one awakens to this mind, then ignorance is itself wisdom;
if one is deluded regarding this mind, then wisdom is itself ignorance.)
"Sūtra" means "path. It is the path for reaching the other shore. As for "sūtra," it signifies "to penetrate" and "to encompass":

it penetrates the meanings that ought to be taught and encompasses those sentient beings who are to be converted. Although more than two thousand years have passed since the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the True Dharma has not been lost;
this is due to the penetration provided by the sūtras. While sentient beings drift through the six realms of existence, they follow the teachings and all return to the right path.
Regarding the structural organization of the sutra, the commentary divides it into three parts: first, the Introduction; second, the Main Body; and third, the Dissemination. Chapter One:
The Section on the Causes and Conditions of the Dharma Assembly.
Pointing out the Path as the Origin of the Dharma Assembly: Those who cultivate the Way fill the rivers and lakes;
If you wish to travel a thousand li, start from the first step. One who treads upon their own mountain home is a true man.
Thus have I heard: at one time the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, together with a great assembly...

The assembly consisted of one thousand two hundred and fifty people. At that time, when it was mealtime, the World-Honored One put on his robes, took up his alms bowl, and entered the great city of Śrāvastī to beg for food.
Having gone through the city begging for food in due order, he returned to his original location.
When he had finished eating, he put away his robes and bowl, washed his feet, spread out a seat, and sat down.
This is the ritual for the Buddha’s dwelling in the world and his preaching of the Dharma. Thus it is said: "Thus have I heard.
Ānanda speaks of himself as having heard this from the Buddha. "At one time" refers to the occasion when teacher and disciple were assembled.
"Buddha" means awakening; he awakens himself and awakens others. "Śrāvastī" is the city where King Prasenajit resided. "Jeta" is the name of the crown prince.
In the language of China, this means "Victory. It was named because it arose from the King’s victory over neighboring states. As for Jeta Grove, it was planted by Prince Jeta.
The Prince relinquished this garden to the Elder Sudatta, who constantly provided for the solitary and the poor;
he built a vihāra within it and invited the Buddha to dwell there and preach the Dharma. Those who heard it together included great bhikṣus and others. This is its name.
"Beggar" (bhikṣu): He begs the Dharma from the Buddha and begs for food from others. "Great" (mahā-): One who is revered and honored by people;
the Buddha speaks the wondrous Truth, which cannot be suddenly realized except by a Great Bhikṣu. "Assembly" (saṃgha): A gathering in harmonious union.
As for the "one thousand two hundred and fifty persons": after the Buddha attained enlightenment, he first delivered the five men, including Kauṇḍinya, and subsequently delivered Kāśyapa.
"Five hundred" refers to five hundred people; later, Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and others—two hundred and fifty people in total—also came to the park to hear the Dharma.
"Together" means that the entire assembly was present; thus, there is no doubt that this sutra was heard directly from the Buddha himself.
"At that time" refers to the moment when he was about to preach the sutra. "World-Honored One" (Bhagavān) is one of his ten titles.
He is fully endowed with merit and wisdom regarding both the mundane and the supramundane. When the Buddha ate at midday, it was the time for his meal; that is, the moment he was about to eat.
He put on his robes, specifically the golden *saṃghāṭī*, a robe of twenty-five strips. His alms bowl was the appropriate vessel. The park was located outside the city;
entering from the outside into the inner city, which was a great metropolis, vast in area and populous. He went forth to beg for alms.
He subdued his own arrogance and shattered the stinginess of others. This sequence was applied regardless of whether one was rich or poor. Originally, he returned to the garden for his meals;
he set aside his robes and purified his bowl, and washed his feet so as not to allow them to become dusty or defiled. He sat in the *paryaṅka* posture, ensuring he did not succumb to fatigue.
The conduct of the Great Sage was no different from that of ordinary people; throughout, his demeanor was characterized by much composure and ease.
If the Three Jewels are not complete, the Dharma assembly cannot be established. Such is the Dharma. The Buddha is present—this is the Buddha. The great bhikṣus—this is the Saṅgha.
Whenever one wishes to propagate the Buddha-Dharma, it relies entirely upon the power of the Three Jewels.

Begging for food is the majestic deportment of the precepts (*śīla*). Spreading the seat and sitting is meditative concentration (*samādhi*). That the World-Honored One himself performed these acts constitutes wisdom (*prajñā*). Thus, there are the precepts, concentration, and wisdom.
This is the untainted study of the Three Jewels.
○ Section Two: Subhūti’s Inquiry.
Regarding the origins of Subhūti’s request for instruction: If one advances upon the Path, why must one seek it outwardly?
The Buddha is fundamentally the mind, and the mind is the Buddha; all of Vulture Peak resides within your own heart.
This entire *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* was initiated by a single question from Subhūti.
At that time, the Elder Subhūti rose from his seat amidst the great assembly.

He bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee upon the ground, joined his palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "It is rare, World-Honored One! The Tathāgata well protects and sustains all bodhisattvas;
he well entrusts all bodhisattvas. World-Honored One, those sons and daughters of good family who have resolved toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*..."
"...the mind set on *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. How should one dwell? How should one subdue the mind?
The Buddha said, "Excellent, excellent, Subhūti! It is as you have said. The Tathāgata well protects and sustains all bodhisattvas;
he well entrusts all bodhisattvas. Listen attentively now, and I shall speak for you. Son of good family, daughter of good family, having generated the [mind set on]..."
“Regarding the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, one should abide thus and thus subdue that mind.
‘So be it, World-Honored One; we wish and desire to hear [your teaching].’”
The Prajñā of true emptiness: one who does not understand emptiness cannot engage in mutual exhortation with the Buddha. Subhūti is foremost in understanding emptiness;

in the language of China, he is called Kūṭadanta (Empty-born), and is also named Shanxian (Well-manifested). When the Tathāgata was sitting cross-legged while begging for food, [Subhūti addressed him as follows].
Although the assembly sat at ease according to the occasion, with neither speaker nor listener, Subhūti suddenly perceived this moment.
Amidst the great multitude, he could no longer restrain his indignation; he rose from his seat, wishing to request the Great Dharma.
First, he assumed a solemn and reverent demeanor, performing the Western rite by baring his right shoulder and placing his right knee on the ground—thus honoring the right.

With palms joined, he single-mindedly upholds [this teaching]. While the great assembly sees only the Tathāgata putting on his robes and begging for food, no different from the common folk, Subhūti alone perceives that which distinguishes him from others.
He is truly the Sole Honored One above and below heaven and earth;
therefore, opening his mouth, he says, "How rare is the World-Honored One! This "rarity" (rareness) has three meanings. First, he is able to...

He renounced the sovereignty of a Golden Wheel-turning King. Second, his body was one zhang and six chi in height, with a complexion like polished purple gold, endowed with the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor characteristics.
Third, his nature was capable of containing and expounding the eighty-four thousand dharmas, and he was fully perfected in the three bodies.
The perfection of both merit and wisdom, along with the protection and entrustment that daily increase in excellence, is brought about through secret and subtle skillful means;

this is indeed a rare and marvelous matter. As Maitreya said: "One should understand the meaning of skillful protection: to augment their practice by acting in concert with them is true self-benefit and benefit for others.
He further stated: "Not falling back from what has been attained and not failing to attain what has not yet been attained—this is called [the stage of non-retrogression]."
"Skillfully entrusted. *Anuttara* means "unexcelled"; *samyak* means "correct"; *saṃbodhi* means "perfectly equal awakening.
Because it is perfectly luminous and shines universally, it is called "Unexcelled, Correct, Equal, and Perfect Awakening. This refers to the awakening to reality through correct wisdom.
Omniscience awakens to the conventional; it is in no way biased or deviant. One who gives rise to this mind abides in what dharma? What kind of mind does one subdue?

If one were to claim there is a reality in which to abide or a deluded mind to be subdued, that would not be the effort of a man or woman seeking to realize the fruit of Buddhahood by giving rise to this mind.
Such effort lies solely in the cultivation of the mind. The cultivation of the mind aims solely at stability. Buddha...
Because he questioned him so earnestly regarding body and mind, [the Buddha] deeply praised his insight and replied: "Not abiding in any single dharma is true abiding;

subduing all minds that grasp at signs is true subduing. Abiding in and subduing these two non-dual dharmas—namely, not abiding in any dharma—is precisely what it means to subdue the mind that grasps at signs.
To subdue the mind that grasps at signs is precisely what it means to not abide."
"All dharmas are, in their entirety, nothing other than this single *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
For one who is thus, it is essential to attain this mind that abides in itself and subdues itself; this is precisely what is meant by 'there is no dharma to be attained and no dharma to be spoken.
All things are encompassed within these two characters. As soon as Wuxing heard these words, he directly realized them and gave his response.
"Indeed, I wish to hear it with joy. There are five kinds of bodhi: first, the bodhi of generating the mind (*cittotpāda-bodhi*), which refers to the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*);

second, the bodhi of subduing the mind (*vinīta-citta-bodhi*), which refers to the three stages of worthiness (*tri-piṭaka-puṇya-kṣetra*); third, the bodhi of realizing the mind (*vidita-citta-bodhi*), which spans from the first to the tenth stage;

fourth, the bodhi of departure and arrival (*niryāṇa-prāpti-bodhi*), which refers to the eighth, ninth, and tenth stages; fifth, the unsurpassed bodhi (*anuttara-bodhi*), which is [the state of] suchness (*tathatā*)."
This is the stage of arrival.
The Second Patriarch attended upon Bodhidharma and requested the Dharma of "settling the mind. Bodhidharma said, "Bring forth your mind, and I shall settle it for you.
The Patriarch replied, "I have searched for my mind, but it is utterly unobtainable. Bodhidharma said, "I have finished settling your mind for you. Thus it was under the gate of the Patriarch.
A single word settles it all; this is why it is called the *zong* (essence). Now, the World-Honored One has expounded many methods for settling the mind;
his compassionate heart has leaked through, and this is why it is called the *jiao* (teaching). In the end, it is simply this: seeking the mind, one finds it is ultimately unobtainable.

Therefore, prior to the Fourth Patriarch, all used the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* to seal the mind; from the Sixth Patriarch at Huangmei onward, all have used the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* to seal the mind.
Thus, this scripture is not a matter of literal words, but resides entirely in the subtlety of transcending speech.
Whenever the scripture asks, "What do you think? it is always turning back to investigate one's doubts.
Having subdued [the mind], one then leaves behind distraction, contempt, and inversion, giving rise to the three types of wisdom—those born of hearing, reflection, and cultivation.
Section Three: The True Principle of the Mahāyāna.
The Mahāyāna’s true principle is not many; the Way is truly beyond words—what can the mind be like?
Do not say that being wordless is itself the Way; you remain, as ever, within the thicket of entanglements.
This chapter answers the subduing [of the mind], and abiding is already contained therein.
The Buddha told Subhūti: "All bodhisattvas, mahāsattvas, should subdue their minds in this way:
'Whatever classes of sentient beings there may be—whether born from eggs, born from wombs, born from moisture, or born by transformation;
whether with form or without form; whether with perception, without perception, or neither with nor without perception—I shall cause them all [to enter parinirvāṇa...]"

He enters *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* and brings them to extinction. Although he thus brings immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless sentient beings to extinction, in reality there are no sentient beings who attain extinction.
Why is this? Subhūti, if a bodhisattva possesses the mark of a self, the mark of a person, the mark of a sentient being, or the mark of a life-span, then he is not a bodhisattva.
This section specifically answers Subhūti’s question regarding the single phrase "subduing one's mind.
It means that this mind cannot be subdued precisely because the categories of sentient beings are so numerous and the four marks [of birth] are difficult to forget.
All classes of sentient beings, though they are immeasurable, innumerable, and boundless, do not exceed the four modes of birth: womb-born, egg-born, moisture-born, and transformation-born.

Regarding birth: within the four modes of birth, there is nothing that does not fall within the two phenomena of body and mind. When discussing the body, it does not exceed the categories of being with form or without form.
When discussing the mind, it does not exceed the categories of having perception or without perception.

One whose preceding thought is pure and whose succeeding thought is pure is called a Bodhisattva. One who does not regress from moment to moment, whose mind remains ever pure even while amidst the toils of worldly existence, is called a Mahāsattva.

The Tathāgata points out that sentient beings throughout the three realms and nine stages each possess the wondrous mind of nirvāṇa, enabling them to personally awaken to and enter the state of *anupadhiśeṣa*.
"Without remainder" (*anupadhiśeṣa*) means being free from habitual tendencies and afflictions. "Nirvāṇa" means perfect purity.
Greed does not arise. To "cross over" means to cross the great ocean of birth and death. The Buddha’s mind is impartial;
he universally wishes that all sentient beings may together enter perfect purity and together cross the great ocean of birth and death.

It is only because ordinary people do not see their own original mind, cling to various appearances, and fail to realize the principle of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) that they are called "sentient beings."
If one is free from this illness, in reality there are no sentient beings who attain extinction (nirvāṇa).
Sentient beings are those born from eggs, wombs, moisture, or transformation; when their sentience is exhausted, they still possess form. When form is exhausted, they still possess perception.

When perception is exhausted, they still possess the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Thus, it depicts that which cannot attain quiescent extinction and cannot attain the remainderless state.
The manner in which a Bodhisattva attains parinirvāṇa is precisely this:
to see through all these various distinctions with a single glance, realizing they possess no self-nature and are entirely empty. All sentient beings are nirvāṇa; all nirvāṇa is sentient beings.
All sentient beings are devoid of sentient beings; all nirvāṇa is devoid of nirvāṇa. The reason it is so is precisely because:

It is simply because the four marks do not exist. Human notions of self, attachment, and aversion are the causal conditions for the four illnesses, and all of these arise from the mark of self (*ātman*).

To think, "I am able to bring sentient beings to extinction," is the mark of self. If one thinks, "I am able to bring them to extinction," there must necessarily be those who are brought to extinction by me;
is this not the mark of person (*pudgala*)? To engage in such calculations and discriminations is to give rise to [the four marks] therein.
First, with a mind of aversion, one does not wish to deliver others; to say, "This is a sentient being," is the mark of a sentient being (*sattva-nimitta*).
Second, with a mind of attachment, one wishes to deliver them; to say, "May you live for a hundred years," is the mark of a self (*ātmagrāha-nimitta*).
To possess these four marks is inverted, deluded conceptualization; how can such a mind be subdued? This is what is called "not right" (*asamyak*).
If one is not a bodhisattva, one is not an awakened one.
To subdue while dwelling in cultivation, and to subdue within that dwelling, is the true crossing over. To subdue while cultivating is non-abiding giving;
this is precisely the departure from marks. Regarding "without remainder," there are two meanings: first, the arising of karmic activity; second, liberation.
Exhausted without remainder. All meritorious deeds and practices are gathered and exhausted without remainder.
Section Four: Non-abiding in Wondrous Practice.
The Seal of Non-abiding in Wondrous Practice: Sealing the Three Thousand Worlds. The Seal that Shatters the Three Thousand Worlds to Reveal the Heavenly Nature.
The crows’ cawing and the magpies’ chirping are fully manifested; where squareness and roundness are attained, remain square and round.
The method for subduing has been fully explained, and the method for abiding has also been fully explained.

Only the two characters "extinction" (mie) and "crossing over" (du) cannot be separated: extinction occurs precisely where there is crossing over, and crossing over occurs precisely where there is extinction.
The six perfections are precisely the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) of nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva should practice giving without dwelling on any phenomenon. That is to say, one should not dwell on form when practicing giving;
one should not dwell on sound, odor, taste, tangibles, or mental phenomena when practicing giving. Subhūti, a bodhisattva should act as follows:
This is giving. Why is it that one does not dwell upon signs? If a bodhisattva practices giving without dwelling upon signs, the merit of that giving is inconceivable and immeasurable.
Subhūti, what do you think? Can the space in the eastern direction be measured or conceived?
"No, World-Honored One. "Subhūti, can the space of the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir be measured?
"No, World-Honored One. "Subhūti, the merit of a bodhisattva’s giving that is without attachment to signs is likewise immeasurable.
Subhūti, a bodhisattva should simply abide in accordance with what has been taught."
This further answers Subhūti’s question regarding how one should abide in the single phrase "how should one dwell.

It means that this mind has not yet attained stable abiding precisely because one performs meritorious deeds while praying for karmic retribution; thus, one cannot avoid being attached to such thoughts. Only a Bodhisattva practices giving within the dharma of non-abiding.
There are three kinds of giving: first, the gift of material wealth (*āmiṣadāna*); second, the gift of fearlessness (*abhayadāna*); and third, the gift of Dharma (*dharmadāna*).
In giving, one does not dwell on sound, form, fragrance, taste, touch, or mental objects.

These three types of non-dwelling mean not only that their marks are absent, but furthermore that the mind itself is absent. When a Bodhisattva practices giving in this manner, all three spheres are empty.
There is no sign to which one may abide. The merit [thereof] is such that it is like the empty space of the ten directions, beyond measure or calculation.
The Bodhisattva’s mind of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment should abide in accordance with this teaching.
In short, there is nothing at all upon which the mind abides, yet there is nowhere the mind does not abide.
Among all things in the world, none is greater than empty space. Among all natures, none is greater than Buddha-nature.
Within this empty space, there is fundamentally no east, west, south, or north; if one perceives east, west, south, or north, this is likewise to dwell in signs (*nimitta*).
Buddha-nature fundamentally lacks the four marks of self, person, sentient being, and life-span; if these four marks can be perceived, then [it is not Buddha-nature].
This is the nature of sentient beings; it is not called the Buddha-nature, namely, giving while abiding in signs. "Ying" (應) means "only.
Only by practicing the teaching as described above—giving while abiding in signlessness—is one a bodhisattva.
The verse of Maitreya says: "The meaning of *dāna* (generosity) encompasses six: material gifts, fearlessness, and the Dharma;
herein, one, two, and three are called the stages of practice and abiding. Regarding "abiding nowhere":
it is not only the single dharma of giving, but even the six *pāramitās*, the four immeasurables, and *bodhi* and *nirvāṇa*—all are without abiding. To abide in non-abiding is as follows:
The empty space of the ten directions. Chapter Five:

Seeing According to Reality as It Is In seeing according to reality as it is, there is fundamentally no differentiation; sages and ordinary beings alike seal it with the same single branch of a flower.
The five petals joined in fragrance have flourished gloriously for a thousand ages;
yet to this day, there are those in the world who boast of the preceding passage about "not dwelling on appearances" without having yet explained the reason why one ought not to dwell on appearances.
One obtains immeasurable merit; this merely speaks of the retribution of merit that is signless (*animitta*).
This pertains to the level of provisional transformation (*nirmāṇa*), and it has never been said that there is a source for signlessness.
As for the statement, "Whatever has signs is all false and illusory," how could one dwell upon such false and illusory phenomena?
"Subhūti, what do you think? Can the Tathāgata be seen by means of his physical marks? No, World-Honored One;
the Tathāgata cannot be seen by means of his physical marks. Why is this? The physical marks spoken of by the Tathāgata are not, in fact, physical marks.
The Buddha told Subhūti: "Whatever marks there may be, they are all empty and illusory. If one sees that all marks are non-marks,"
He immediately beheld the Tathāgata.
This section examines and verifies the previous teaching on giving without attachment to marks.

If even the Buddha, who possesses the thirty-two marks, is yet "not a mark," how much more so should one not be attached to marks when practicing giving? In short, the wondrous practice of signlessness does not reside in the Buddha.

Regarding the marks of transformation and response, one should instead perceive the true essence of the Dharmakāya. The World-Honored One directly declared that the Tathāgata cannot be seen by means of marks;
for the body spoken of by the Tathāgata is precisely the Dharmakāya, and is therefore called "non-body."
That which is "non-characteristic" is the unconditioned essence of the Tathāgata’s awakening. Since it is called "unconditioned," how can it be seen?
It is because sentient beings, due solely to deluded thoughts, give rise to all manner of discrimination;
thus they perceive the various characteristics of delusion and fail to see the true reality of non-characteristic. If deluded thoughts do not arise, discrimination will suddenly vanish.
Then the essence of true awakening manifests spontaneously; for this reason, it is said that one "sees the Tathāgata.

it cannot be described to others, and is merely designated by the provisional name "patience" (*kṣānti*). Upon reaching this realm...
How could the causal fruits of such merit be equaled by mere giving? Furthermore, how could it be the same as the greedy attachment of ordinary worldlings?
"Patience" (kṣānti) possesses the sense of approval; one enters [the path] from receiving this sutra. "Patience" possesses the sense of stability; one [proceeds] from upholding this...

Entering through the Sūtras, Wang Kuangshi said: "In the Mahāprajñāpāramitā, there are the patience of receptive endurance (*anupādāna-kṣānti*) and the patience of analytical observation (*vipaśyanā-kṣānti*).

By cultivating these two types of patience, one attains the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). Once the power of patience is perfected, one spontaneously attains the bliss of non-arising; therefore, it is said that 'one attains perfection.'"
Chapter Twenty-nine: The Tranquility of Dignified Manner The tranquility of dignified manner transcends the three mysteries;
In every particle of dust, the sky beneath the water is revealed.
The flying staff holds the sun and moon at its tip; Within a single pore, the three thousandfold world-system is contained.

This chapter sweeps away the traces of the indeterminate nature of the *saṃbhogakāya* (enjoyment body) and points out the Tathāgata’s eternally quiescent *dharmakāya* (dharma body) to show it to people.
Subhūti, if anyone were to say that the Tathāgata comes or goes, sits or lies down, that person...
Understand the meaning of what I have said. Why is this? The Tathāgata comes from nowhere and goes nowhere;
therefore, he is called the Tathāgata.
The previous statement that one cannot perceive him by means of marks meant that the Tathāgata does not abide in existence. The subsequent statement that he does not teach annihilation means:
"Extinction. The Tathāgata does not abide in non-existence. Yet, if one cannot penetrate the single source within the Dharma-body, how could one understand the meaning of what I have taught?
That which is called the 'Tathāgata' does not take manifested transformation as its body;
it takes the Dharma-nature as its body. The entire Dharma-realm is the substance of suchness, eternally unmoving, fundamentally without coming or going."

When it comes, because the minds of sentient beings are pure, it appears as soon as the conditions arise. When it departs, because the minds of sentient beings are defiled, it vanishes once the stimulus has ended.
It is like the moon appearing when water is clear—the moon does not come; and the moon disappearing when water is turbid—the moon does not go.
Thus we know that the Dharmakāya, the true Buddha, is in essence devoid of coming and going. Because it does not come, it is free from all things.
The Dharma, because it does not depart, is itself all phenomena.
If it manifests as the four modes of conduct, it is nothing other than the traces manifested for the purpose of transforming and delivering sentient beings. How could this be called the Tathāgata?
Chapter Thirty-one: Harmonizing with the Principle of Reality In the fundamental nature of reality, there is originally no duality. The path is one of equality toward both enemies and kin;
whether square or round, whether perverse or correct, all are but manifestations of the essence. Vast and unconfined, one rejoices in spontaneity.
To break the unity of a composite is to break conceptual differentiation;
this is self-evident. Subhūti, suppose a good man or a good woman were to grind the trichiliocosm into fine dust.
What do you think? Would that mass of atoms be numerous? Subhūti replied, "It would be very many, World-Honored One."
"World-Honored One, why is this? If these multitudes of subtle atoms were truly existent, the Buddha would not have called them 'multitudes of subtle atoms. Why is that?
What the Buddha calls 'multitudes of subtle atoms' is not actually a multitude of subtle atoms; it is merely designated as 'a multitude of subtle atoms.'"
The Buddha spoke of the trichiliocosm as a metaphor for the number of motes of dust upon the nature of each and every sentient being.
Just as there are all the motes of dust within the trichiliocosm, so too do all sentient beings hear the sutra and awaken to the Way;
their enlightened wisdom constantly shines as they advance toward Bodhi, with every thought-moment remaining unceasing and always abiding in purity. As it is said:
These are pure atoms; this is what is called a multitude of atoms. Aggregates of dust form realms, and breaking down realms results in dust.
Originally, they have no substantial reality. If they possessed substantial reality, one could speak of them as real.
Because he manifests throughout the ten directions, he is not one; because he relies upon a single essence, he is not many.
World-Honored One, that which the Tathāgata calls the "trichiliocosm" is not a world; it is merely named a "world."
Why is this? If a world were truly existent, it would be a "unified mass" (*piṇḍa-grāha*).
That which the Tathāgata calls a unified mass is not a unified mass; it is merely designated as a unified mass. Subhūti, that which is a unified mass is ineffable;
yet ordinary people greedily cling to it as a thing.
The Dharma-body of the Tathāgata neither comes nor goes; it is like the three thousand great thousandfold worlds combined to form a single realm.

When the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata manifests as the response-body (nirmāṇakāya), it appears to come and go; this is like the three thousand great thousandfold worlds being shattered into fine motes of dust.
Although the Tathāgata has posed this question regarding the multitude of these motes of dust, his underlying intent is to reveal [the nature of the Dharma-body].

The elements and sense-objects lack substantial nature. When the Tathāgata speaks of a "unified whole" (*ekapiṇḍa-lakṣaṇa*), he does so precisely from the perspective of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
The one true *dharmadhātu* is equal, perfectly interfused, and cannot be grasped as a mass of material forms; it cannot be reached by the mind or intellect.
The *dharmakāya* and the *nirmāṇakāya* have no priority or posteriority; they are neither cause nor effect. At times, [the Master] would take up...
Within a single atom, the entire realm is perfectly manifest; yet at times, a thousand realms appear while not a single atom is established. One is all, and all is one.
Who is the agent that joins, and what is the object joined, such that a "unified appearance" (*ekasamagraha-lakṣaṇa*) is formed?
This is merely because ordinary beings cling to phenomena on the level of appearances, perceiving all myriad dharmas as being composed of distinct parts.

Thus they combine; from the many, they become one. To grasp at the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) and to seize upon their conjunction is a matter of greedy attachment. These five aggregates in conjunction have no substantial reality.

In sum, the elements (*dhātu*) resolve into the sense objects (*viṣaya*), yet there are no elements to be grasped. The sense objects resolve into consciousness (*vijñāna*), yet there are no sense objects to be grasped.
The four aggregates are free from thought; there is no mind to be grasped. That sentient beings grasp and cling is entirely due to...
False conceptualization consists in perceiving the five aggregates and failing to understand the emptiness of phenomena; this is attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*).

To grasp at the combination [of causes and conditions] without penetrating all phenomena is attachment to a self (*ātman-grāha*). Because these two attachments are not forgotten, one is said to be greedily attached to those things.

Asuṅga said: "In order to destroy the conception of a physical body (rūpakāya), the realms and so forth are taught. Within this, there are the method of subtle pulverization and the method of non-perception.

'The realms are exceedingly numerous' refers to the method of subtle pulverization. The Buddha’s intention is that the realms are used as a metaphor for the true body (dharmakāya), while the particles (rajas) are used as a metaphor for the transformation body (nirmāṇakāya).
The Tathāgata would rather say that [the world] is ground into subtle dust than say that it is joined together to form a world."
The Realm. As soon as one speaks of "one," it immediately falls into "two" and "three. As soon as one speaks of "union," distinctions are formed.
Chapter Thirty-one: The Non-arising of Knowledge and Vision.
Knowledge and vision do not arise; clouds obscure the moon. Suddenly hearing the wind sweep them away, the full orb appears.
The radiance shines brightly throughout heaven and earth, Illuminating the three thousandfold world-systems and the great chiliocosm.
This chapter demonstrates the Buddha’s knowledge and vision— the knowledge and vision that is "seeing through non-seeing"—
and entrusts the Bodhisattvas to abide in right view.
Subhūti, if someone were to say that the Buddha has taught the view of a self, the view of a person, the view of a sentient being, or the view of a life-span—Subhūti, what do you think?
Would such a person understand the meaning of what I have taught? "No, World-Honored One; such a person does not understand the meaning of what the Tathāgata has taught.
Why is this? Because the World-Honored One has said: "the view of a self, the view of a person, the view of a sentient being, the view of a life-span..."

To have such views is not to have the view of a self, the view of a person, the view of a sentient being, or the view of a life-span. These are what are called the view of a self, the view of a person, the view of a sentient being, and the view of a life-span.
When the Tathāgata says that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature, this is the view of a true self (*ātman*).
When he says that all sentient beings are inherently endowed with the nature of untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*), this is the view of a person (*pudgala*).

When he says that all sentient beings are fundamentally free from afflictions (*kleśa*), this is called the view of sentient beings (*sattva*). When he says that the nature of all sentient beings is fundamentally neither born nor extinguished, this is...
This is called the view of a self.

Subhūti, those who have set their minds on *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* should, regarding all phenomena (*dharma*), know them thus, see them thus, and resolve with faith thus, so that they do not give rise to the conceptualization of phenomena. Subhūti, as for what is called "phenomena"...
Regarding "characteristics": the Tathāgata has said that what is called a characteristic of dharmas is not actually a characteristic of dharmas; this is termed the "characteristic of dharmas.
Regarding all dharmas, one should understand their principles clearly as stated in the sūtras, discern them through such vision, and gain insight and realization through such faith.
In this way, the characteristic of dharmas will no longer arise. When dharmas reach [this state]—
At the moment of awakening, dharmas are no longer required; how then could there still be the characteristics of dharmas? Therefore it is said, "It is not," and "This is merely a name.
To say that the characteristics of dharmas do not arise means not grasping or clinging to dharmas. What the Tathāgata has spoken is intended to sweep away the views of sentient beings and empty them;
it is not to establish his own views as a standard. If sentient beings were without [views]...
Regarding this view, even the Tathāgata has never made such a statement. In sum, when conceptual discrimination does not arise, from what could the various marks (lakṣaṇa) possibly emerge?
Not only is there no mark of self (ātma-lakṣaṇa), but there is also no mark of phenomena (dharma-lakṣaṇa); nor is there even the absence of the mark of non-phenomena.
Furthermore, the very view of "non-existence" is itself absent. To know and perceive with such faith and understanding is precisely what is meant by "thus subduing."
I prostrate. Thus he dwells in peace.
Chapter Thirty-two: Manifestations Are Not Real.
Manifestations encompass past and present; responding to conditions in the world, they are fundamentally without mind.
A single thread of spiritual resonance beyond the Sound of Majesty; the Master Without Mouth chants day and night.
Generally, when one speaks of "upholding" (dhāraṇī), it necessarily implies speaking it for others.

While the methods for receiving and upholding have been explained exhaustively within the sutras, the methods for expounding them have not yet been clarified; therefore, they are shown at the end of the sutra as an entrustment.
The Entrustment:
"Subhūti, if someone were to take seven treasures filling immeasurable asaṃkhyeya worlds and offer them as a gift,
and if there were a son of good family or a daughter of good family who has resolved upon bodhicitta and holds this sūtra, even..."
If one receives, maintains, reads, recites, and explains even as little as a four-line verse for others, their merit will surpass that of the former.
How does one explain it for others? Without grasping at signs, remaining as suchness, unmoving.

Although the merit of the seven treasures may be great, it is not equal to that of a person who gives rise to the bodhicitta, receives and upholds even four lines of this sutra, and expounds them for others;
the latter’s merit surpasses the former. Such a person employs skillful means in preaching the Dharma, observing the faculties of others and acting according to their measure.
Adapting in various ways to what is appropriate is called "expounding for people. As for those who listen to the Dharma, they possess various and unequal characteristics;

one must not harbor a discriminating mind toward them. Rather, one should realize the mind of emptiness and stillness, the mind of suchness (*tathatā*), the mind of non-attainment, the mind free from grasping, rejecting, victory, or defeat, the mind free from expectation, and the mind free from arising and ceasing. This is called "suchness" (*yathābhūta*).
It is like an unshakable mind.
Asasaṅga says: "Because one preaches the Dharma without being defiled, and because there is such great benefit, one resolutely expounds it.
To expound in this way is itself to be undefiled."
Why is this? The Buddha ought to remain permanently in the world to preach the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings; why then does he enter nirvana?
Fearing that people might give rise to doubt, the following verse provides the explanation.
"All conditioned phenomena are like a dream, an illusion, a bubble, and a shadow; they are like dew and like lightning—thus should one regard them.
At the conclusion of the sutra, he again reminds [the assembly] of the four-line verse and so forth, all of which signify that the myriad dharmas return to emptiness.
This precisely serves to conclude the intent that all marks are non-marks, saying: "Do not grasp at marks," thereby summarizing that all marks are empty and false to bring about full understanding.
The meaning of being free from marks is precisely the meaning of Buddhahood; it is called "suchness, immovable.
This summarizes the mind that dwells nowhere, thereby clarifying the meaning of abiding and subduing. Furthermore, one applies six kinds of contemplation to all phenomena.
When this contemplation is thoroughly penetrating, one naturally views all things as empty. Within this, there is entirely and solely *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Why would the mind not abide in peace? Why wait for it to be subdued? Contemplation is precisely the wondrous wisdom of *prajñā*.

Since that which contemplates is wondrous wisdom, that which is contemplated is nothing other than the wondrous realm. To contemplate in this way is to realize that the *nirmāṇakāya* is itself the *dharmakāya*.
The Dharmakāya is unimpeded by nirvāṇa.
It is like a dream, like an illusion, like a bubble, like a shadow, like dew, and like lightning. For one who has awakened to the mind, [all things] arise in accordance with the nature;
they are spontaneously accomplished without effort and arise according to conditions. Once the conditions pass, they are immediately stilled. How could there ever be even a hair’s breadth of reality?
The Dharma may allow for people to dwell in attachment; yet, by awakening to true emptiness, one does not dwell in signs, and by observing arising and ceasing, one is exhorted to practice.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the Elder Subhūti, along with the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, [and upāsikās], [were filled with joy and faith].
Upāsikā, all those in the world—gods, humans, and asuras—hearing what the Buddha had spoken, were all greatly rejoiced;
they believed, accepted, and practiced it accordingly.

This took place at Jetavana. Having finished preaching the sutra, among all those in the world—gods, humans, and even the most fierce classes of ghosts and spirits—who was not struck with awe by the ocean of suffering that is saṃsāra?
Everyone joyfully turned their heads toward the Buddha. Such is the power of the Buddha’s Dharma to move the hearts of beings.
The scribe has finished recording the sutra. Each time it was spoken, all were filled with great joy. They believed, accepted, and practiced it.

For if one believes and accepts but does not practice, then even that belief and acceptance is in vain; what benefit is there in mere joy? This is the case for those in the world who merely uphold the sutra.
One should exert oneself with vigorous introspection at this point.
*The Diamond Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* (concluded).
